hints: Think about where excess fertiliser goes when it rains, and what nitrates do to water plants.
Remember that leached $\text{NO}_3^-$ ions act as nutrients in rivers and cause eutrophication and algal blooms.
Now ask yourself if fertiliser in soil creates the sunny, traffic-pollution mix needed for photochemical smog.
walkthrough:
**Follow the excess fertiliser**

Think like the rainwater. Too much $\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$ on the field does not all stay in the soil.

It dissolves and leaches, so $\text{NO}_3^-$ ions wash into nearby rivers and lakes.

**Link nitrates to river growth**

Nitrate is a key plant nutrient. In water it acts just like fertiliser for algae and water plants.

$$\text{excess } \text{NO}_3^- \text{ in water} \rightarrow \text{eutrophication} \rightarrow \text{algal bloom}$$

**Check photochemical smog**

Photochemical smog is a different story. It needs nitrogen oxides ($\text{NO}_x$), volatile organic compounds and strong sunlight, mainly from car exhausts in cities.

Adding solid fertiliser to soil does not directly make this smog, so increased river growth is yes and photochemical smog is no.

options.A: Incorrect. It says no increased plant growth in rivers. This misses eutrophication, the classic effect where leached nitrates fertilise algae and cause blooms and oxygen loss.
options.B: Correct and well done. Leached nitrate causes eutrophication, so increased plant growth in rivers is true. Photochemical smog from traffic pollution is not caused by fertiliser use, so that is false.
options.C: Incorrect. It gets both columns backwards. It denies eutrophication and wrongly links fertiliser to photochemical smog, which comes from $\text{NO}_x$ and hydrocarbons in sunlight, not from soil fertiliser.
options.D: Half right, half wrong. It correctly includes increased river plant growth, but wrongly adds photochemical smog. Students choosing this often confuse all nitrogen pollution problems as the same thing.
